title: UNIT 5: HUMAN BIOLOGY
notes: ✓ Human biology studies the structure and functions of the human body and how its organ systems work together to maintain life.

title: 5.1 DIGESTIVE SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The digestive system breaks food into smaller molecules that can be absorbed and used by body cells. It has two major parts:

→ Alimentary canal → mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus.
→ Accessory organs → salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas.

✓ Main processes: ingestion → digestion → absorption → elimination.

title: FUNCTIONS OF THE DIGESTIVE SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The major tasks of digestion are:
1 Ingestion → taking food into the mouth.
2 Mechanical digestion → physically breaking food into smaller pieces.
3 Chemical digestion → enzymes break large molecules into smaller molecules.
4 Motility → movement of food through the digestive tract.
5 Absorption → nutrients, minerals, vitamins and water enter the body.
6 Elimination → undigested materials leave the body.

title: TEETH & DIGESTION
notes:
✓ Teeth perform mechanical digestion by cutting, tearing and grinding food.

◆ Incisors → cutting food.
◆ Canines → tearing food.
◆ Premolars → crushing and grinding.
◆ Molars → grinding food.

→ The main parts of a tooth include enamel, dentine, pulp, cementum and the root.

title: MOUTH, PHARYNX & ESOPHAGUS
notes:
→ Mouth → receives food; chewing begins mechanical digestion and saliva begins carbohydrate digestion.

→ Pharynx → passage shared by food and air; helps move swallowed food toward the esophagus.

→ Esophagus → muscular tube that moves food toward the stomach by rhythmic contractions called peristalsis.

✓ Peristalsis allows food to move even against gravity.

title: STOMACH
notes:
✓ The stomach is a muscular organ that stores and mixes food.

◆ Mechanical digestion → muscular contractions mix food.
◆ Hydrochloric acid (HCl) → creates an acidic environment and helps kill microbes.
◆ Pepsinogen → converted to pepsin, which begins protein digestion.
◆ Mucus → protects the stomach lining from acid and digestive enzymes.

→ The partially digested food forms a semi-liquid mixture before entering the small intestine.

title: ACCESSORY ORGANS
notes:
◆ Salivary glands → produce saliva containing salivary amylase.
◆ Liver → produces bile and performs important metabolic functions.
◆ Gallbladder → stores and concentrates bile.
◆ Pancreas → releases digestive enzymes and bicarbonate ions into the small intestine.

✓ These organs assist digestion but food does not pass through them.

title: DIGESTIVE ENZYMES & SECRETIONS
notes:
◆ Salivary amylase → begins carbohydrate digestion.
◆ HCl → activates pepsinogen to pepsin and kills microbes.
◆ Pepsin → begins protein digestion.
◆ Pancreatic amylase → continues carbohydrate digestion.
◆ Trypsin → breaks proteins/peptides into smaller peptides.
◆ Pancreatic lipase → breaks fats into glycerol and fatty acids.
◆ Erepsin → completes protein digestion.
◆ Disaccharidases such as maltase → break disaccharides into monosaccharides.
◆ Bile → emulsifies fats, increasing their surface area for lipase action.
◆ Bicarbonate ions → neutralize stomach acid in the small intestine.

title: END PRODUCTS OF DIGESTION
notes:
◆ Carbohydrates → monosaccharides, mainly glucose.
◆ Proteins → amino acids.
◆ Fats/lipids → fatty acids and glycerol.

✓ These small molecules can be absorbed and used by body cells.

title: SMALL INTESTINE & ABSORPTION
notes:
✓ The small intestine is the main site of digestion and absorption. Its inner surface has numerous folds and villi that greatly increase the surface area for absorption.

◆ Capillaries → absorb glucose, amino acids, minerals and water-soluble substances.
◆ Lacteals → absorb many products of fat digestion.

✓ Villi provide a large surface area and a short pathway for efficient absorption.

title: LARGE INTESTINE & ELIMINATION
notes:
✓ The large intestine absorbs remaining water and helps form feces. Mucus assists movement of waste.

→ The rectum stores feces temporarily, while the anus controls their elimination from the body.

title: 5.2 CIRCULATORY & LYMPHATIC SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes throughout the body. It consists mainly of the heart, blood and blood vessels.

→ The lymphatic system collects excess tissue fluid, returns it to the blood and contributes to immune defense.

title: BLOOD
notes:
✓ Blood is a connective tissue that transports substances throughout the body.

◆ Red blood cells (erythrocytes) → transport oxygen using haemoglobin.
◆ White blood cells (leukocytes) → defend the body against infection.
◆ Plasma → liquid part that transports dissolved substances.
◆ Platelets → help blood clot and reduce blood loss.

title: HEART STRUCTURE
notes:
✓ The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers:

→ Right atrium → receives blood returning from the body.
→ Right ventricle → pumps blood to the lungs.
→ Left atrium → receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.
→ Left ventricle → pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body.

◆ Heart wall layers:
• Epicardium
• Myocardium
• Endocardium

✓ Valves prevent backward flow of blood.

title: DOUBLE CIRCULATION
notes:
→ Pulmonary circulation → right ventricle → lungs → left atrium. It carries blood between the heart and lungs.

→ Systemic circulation → left ventricle → body tissues → right atrium. It carries blood between the heart and the rest of the body.

✓ The two circuits work together to continuously supply tissues with oxygen and nutrients.

title: BLOOD VESSELS
notes:
◆ Arteries → carry blood away from the heart; thick, strong walls withstand high pressure.

◆ Veins → carry blood toward the heart; generally have thinner walls and valves that help prevent backflow.

◆ Capillaries → tiny vessels with very thin walls where exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes occurs.

→ Substances can cross capillary walls through diffusion, filtration and osmosis.

title: HEART CONDUCTION SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The heart has specialized cardiac muscle cells that coordinate its contractions.

→ Electrical signals control the rhythmic contraction of the atria and ventricles, allowing blood to be pumped efficiently through the pulmonary and systemic circuits.

title: 5.2.2 DISEASES OF THE CIRCULATORY & LYMPHATIC SYSTEMS
notes:
◆ Leukemia → cancer affecting blood-forming tissues and producing abnormal blood cells.

◆ Varicose veins → enlarged, twisted veins commonly caused by weakened or faulty valves that allow blood to pool.

◆ Elephantiasis → severe swelling of body parts caused by obstruction of lymphatic drainage, commonly associated with parasitic infection.

◆ Cardiovascular diseases → diseases affecting the heart and blood vessels. Examples include atherosclerosis, hypertension and other heart diseases.

✓ Risk factors can include unhealthy diet, smoking, physical inactivity and other lifestyle factors.

title: LYMPHATIC SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The lymphatic system is an open system of lymph vessels, lymph nodes and lymphatic organs.

◆ Lymph → fluid collected from tissues.
◆ Lymphatic vessels → transport lymph toward the bloodstream.
◆ Lymph nodes → filter lymph and contain immune cells.
◆ Lymphatic organs → include structures such as the spleen and thymus.

✓ Main functions:
• Return excess tissue fluid to the blood.
• Transport absorbed fats from the intestine through lacteals.
• Defend the body against microorganisms and foreign substances.

title: 5.3 BREATHING SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The breathing/respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide.
→ It works closely with the circulatory system to transport gases between the lungs and body tissues.

✓ Main pathway:
Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → smaller airways → alveoli.

title: PARTS OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
notes:
◆ Nose → receives and conditions incoming air.
◆ Pharynx → passage for air.
◆ Larynx → voice box; connects pharynx and trachea.
◆ Trachea → main airway/windpipe.
◆ Bronchi → two main branches leading to the lungs.
◆ Bronchioles → smaller branches of the bronchial tree.
◆ Alveoli → tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.
◆ Lungs → contain the bronchial tree and alveoli.

title: BREATHING & RESPIRATION
notes:
◆ Ventilation → movement of air into and out of the lungs.
◆ External respiration → gas exchange between alveoli and blood.
◆ Gas transport → oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported by blood.
◆ Internal respiration → gas exchange between blood and body tissues.
◆ Cellular respiration → cells use oxygen to release energy from food while producing carbon dioxide and water.

title: MECHANISM OF BREATHING
notes:
→ Inhalation → diaphragm contracts and moves downward; chest volume increases and air enters the lungs.

→ Exhalation → diaphragm relaxes; chest volume decreases and air leaves the lungs.

✓ Changes in chest volume and pressure drive the movement of air.

title: 5.4 EXCRETORY SYSTEM
notes:
✓ The excretory system removes metabolic wastes and helps maintain the body's internal balance.

✓ Major functions include:
◆ Removing waste products.
◆ Controlling body-fluid volume.
◆ Maintaining electrolyte concentrations.
◆ Regulating blood pH.
◆ Producing/secreting substances such as erythropoietin and renin.

→ Main organs: kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.

title: KIDNEY STRUCTURE
notes:
✓ The kidney is the main organ of the urinary system.

◆ Cortex → outer region of the kidney.
◆ Medulla → inner region containing structures involved in urine formation.
◆ Renal pelvis → central collecting region where urine is gathered before entering the ureter.

✓ The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron.

title: NEPHRON
notes:
✓ A nephron consists of a renal corpuscle and a renal tubule.

◆ Renal corpuscle → includes the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule; filtration begins here.

◆ Renal tubule → modifies the filtrate through reabsorption and secretion.

→ The renal tubule includes the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule, followed by connection to collecting ducts.

title: URINE FORMATION
notes:
✓ Urine formation involves three major processes:

1 Filtration → blood is filtered in the renal corpuscle.
2 Selective reabsorption → useful water and substances are returned to the blood.
3 Secretion → additional wastes and excess substances are transferred into the tubule.

→ Final urine passes from the kidney → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra → outside the body.

title: URINARY SYSTEM
notes:
◆ Kidneys → filter blood and produce urine.
◆ Ureters → transport urine from kidneys to the bladder.
◆ Urinary bladder → temporarily stores urine.
◆ Urethra → carries urine out of the body.

✓ Two sphincters regulate urine passage: an involuntary internal urethral sphincter and a voluntary external urethral sphincter.

title: 5.5 IMMUNE SYSTEM
notes: ✓ The immune system protects the body against microorganisms, foreign substances and abnormal cells. It works closely with the lymphatic system and uses specialized cells and chemical defenses.

title: INNATE IMMUNITY
notes:
✓ Innate immunity is the body's initial, non-specific defense against invading pathogens.

◆ Physical and chemical barriers prevent entry of pathogens.
◆ Chemical signals such as cytokines attract immune cells to infection sites.
◆ Complement proteins help recognize and clear pathogens and damaged cells.
◆ Specialized white blood cells identify and remove foreign substances.

→ Innate immunity acts quickly and does not develop specific memory.

title: ADAPTIVE (ACQUIRED) IMMUNITY
notes:
✓ Adaptive immunity develops after exposure to a particular pathogen and produces a targeted response.

◆ Recognizes specific non-self antigens.
◆ Produces targeted responses against pathogens or infected cells.
◆ Creates immunological memory.
◆ Memory cells allow a faster and stronger response during later exposure.

→ Vaccination uses this immune-memory principle to help protect against certain diseases.

title: CELLS OF THE IMMUNE SYSTEM
notes:
◆ Lymphocytes → include T cells, B cells and natural killer cells; important in immune defense.
◆ Neutrophils → common white blood cells that engulf and destroy pathogens and cellular debris.
◆ Macrophages → phagocytes involved in both innate and adaptive immune responses.
◆ Dendritic cells → antigen-presenting cells that connect innate and adaptive immunity and activate lymphocytes.

title: ANTIGENS & ANTIBODIES
notes:
→ Antigen → a foreign substance recognized by the immune system as non-self.

→ Antibody → Y-shaped protein produced by B cells that binds specifically to an antigen. This helps identify the foreign substance and supports its removal.

✓ Antigen = target | Antibody = specific defense protein.

title: IMMUNE SYSTEM & HORMONES
notes:
✓ The immune system produces signaling molecules called lymphokines that help coordinate immune responses.

→ Hormonal and chemical signals influence immune activity and help regulate the body's responses to infection and inflammation.
